extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers seeking an overview of misinformation about Ebola
extracted.subtask_description: A topical Wikipedia article cataloging and summarizing conspiracy theories, hoaxes, and false treatments circulated about Ebola viruses, with examples and cited sources. It describes categories of misinformation (treatments, prevention methods, origin theories) and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple conspiracy theories, hoaxes, and quack cures
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple conspiracy theories, hoaxes, and quack cures have circulated about ebola viruses, regarding the origin of outbreaks, treatments for ebola virus disease, and preventative measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This opening summary frames the article's scope: misinformation about Ebola spans claims about origins, alleged cures/treatments, and prevention methods. Use cited examples in subsequent sections to illustrate each category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unproven and disproven treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: During the Western African Ebola virus epidemic (2013–2016), a number of unproven and fake treatments were marketed online in the United States, including snake venom, vitamin C, 'Nano Silver', and various homeopathic and herbal remedies, including clove oil, garlic, and ewedu soup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited (NPR, CNN, BMJ, LA Times) and an FDA official quote (Gary Coody) are used to document such treatments. The page emphasizes harms beyond inefficacy: these remedies may lead patients to delay effective and timely medical care in a hospital setting. Note both the specific marketed products and the public-health consequences when evaluating such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implausible and disproven methods for preventing Ebola
rubrics_metrics.description: During the 2014 and 2019 outbreaks, a number of hoax remedies for the prevention of Ebola were spread online. One such common thread was the frequent use of essential oils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states: 'There is no evidence that any of these treatments will decrease the risk of Ebola virus infection, and no known plausible mechanisms for such an effect.' Use of examples (essential oils) and explicit statement about lack of evidence and mechanism serve as criteria for labeling prevention claims as misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virus origins (conspiracy theories about origin and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various theories circulated alleging the virus was a bioweapon designed by the US military as a form of population control; that the New World Order engineered the virus to impose quarantines and travel bans; or that the virus was imported for financial gain or as part of a plot to procure organs for the black market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists specific origin-related conspiracy narratives reported in media coverage (Liberian Observer, NYT, NBC, Time) and situates them as rumors and theories undermining outbreak response. When evaluating origin claims, the page treats them as misinformation when they lack credible evidence and when they align with conspiratorial motifs (bioweapon, New World Order, organ-harvesting, profiteering).
